01.title: Introduction to System Calls
01.content:
What is a System Call?

A system call is a mechanism by which a program requests privileged operations from the kernel.

System Call Path

When a program makes a system call, the following happens:

  1. The program puts the system call number into the eax register
  2. The int 0x80 instruction is executed (or syscall on x86_64)
  3. The kernel intercepts the interrupt and calls the appropriate handler
  4. After execution, the result is returned in eax

User Space and Kernel Space

The operating system divides memory into two areas:

  • User Space — where applications run
  • Kernel Space — where the kernel runs

Transition between them is only possible through system calls.

Why Intercept System Calls?

  • Application activity monitoring
  • Debugging and profiling
  • Security (antivirus, firewalls)
  • Modifying system behavior

02.title: sys_call_table Structure
02.content:
System Call Table

The sys_call_table stores addresses of all system call handlers.

Table Structure

It is an array where each index corresponds to a system call number, and the value is the handler function address:

unsigned long *sys_call_table[] = {
  [0] = sys_restart_syscall,
  [1] = sys_exit,
  [2] = sys_fork,
  [3] = sys_read,
  [4] = sys_write,
  // ...
};

How It Works

  1. The program calls system call with number NR_write = 4
  2. The kernel takes the address from sys_call_table[4]
  3. Control is passed to the sys_write function

Where to Find the Table

In the /boot/System.map-$(uname -r) file, you can find the address:

grep sys_call_table /boot/System.map-$(uname -r)

64-bit System Features

On x86_64, there are two tables:

  • sys_call_table — for 64-bit calls
  • ia32_sys_call_table — for 32-bit compatibility

03.title: Kernel Module Development
03.content:
Linux Kernel Modules

A kernel module is code that can be loaded and unloaded into the kernel while the system is running.

Module Structure

#include <linux/init.h>
#include <linux/module.h>
#include <linux/kernel.h>

static int init(void) {
  printk(KERN_ALERT "Hello, Kernel!\n");
  return 0;
}

static void exit(void) {
  printk(KERN_ALERT "Goodbye, Kernel!\n");
}

module_init(init);
module_exit(exit);
MODULE_LICENSE("GPL");

Makefile for Building

obj-m += hello.o

all:
  make -C /lib/modules/$(shell uname -r)/build M=$(PWD) modules

clean:
  make -C /lib/modules/$(shell uname -r)/build M=$(PWD) clean

Working with the Module

  • Load: sudo insmod hello.ko
  • Check: lsmod | grep hello
  • Unload: sudo rmmod hello
  • View logs: dmesg | tail

04.title: Direct Handler Substitution
04.content:
Direct Address Substitution in sys_call_table

This is the simplest and most visual way to intercept system calls.

Algorithm

  1. Find the sys_call_table address
  2. Disable memory page protection (clear CR0 WP-bit)
  3. Save the original handler address
  4. Write your function address to the table
  5. Re-enable protection

Write System Call Substitution Code

unsigned long *syscall_table = (unsigned long *)0xc05d3180;
asmlinkage int (*original_write)(unsigned int, const char __user *, size_t);

asmlinkage int new_write(unsigned int fd, const char __user *buf, size_t count) {
  printk(KERN_ALERT "WRITE HIJACKED\n");
  return (*original_write)(fd, buf, count);
}

static int init(void) {
  write_cr0(read_cr0() & (~0x10000));
  original_write = (void *)syscall_table[__NR_write];
  syscall_table[__NR_write] = (unsigned long)new_write;
  write_cr0(read_cr0() | 0x10000);
  return 0;
}

Important Points

  • asmlinkage — required for system calls
  • CR0 WP-bit — memory page protection
  • Restoration — required when unloading the module

05.title: open Interception. Getting Filename
05.content:
Intercepting open and Getting the Filename

In this module, we'll learn how to intercept the open system call and get the name of the file being opened.

Problem: Copying from User Space

The filename is in user memory. You cannot simply dereference the pointer from the kernel.

Solution: strncpy_from_user

asmlinkage int new_open(const char __user *filename, int flags, umode_t mode) {
  char fname[256];
  
  if (strncpy_from_user(fname, filename, sizeof(fname) - 1) > 0) {
    printk(KERN_ALERT "Opening file: %s\n", fname);
  }
  
  return (*original_open)(filename, flags, mode);
}

open Arguments

  • filename — file name (in user space)
  • flags — open flags (O_RDONLY, O_WRONLY, O_RDWR...)
  • mode — access permissions (for file creation)

06.title: Dynamic Address Resolution
06.content:
Dynamic Address Resolution of sys_call_table

A hardcoded address is bad because when the kernel is updated, the address changes.

Dynamic Search Algorithm

  1. Determine the kernel version
  2. Build the path: /boot/System.map-kernel_version
  3. Open the file and find the line with sys_call_table
  4. Extract the address and convert to a number

Getting the Kernel Version

#include <linux/utsname.h>

static int init(void) {
  printk(KERN_INFO "Kernel version: %s\n", init_uts_ns.name.release);
  return 0;
}

Reading System.map from the Kernel

struct file *f = filp_open("/boot/System.map-2.6.35-24-generic", O_RDONLY, 0);
char buf[1024];
kernel_read(f, 0, buf, 1024);
filp_close(f, current->files);

// Parse the line, find sys_call_table
unsigned long addr = simple_strtoul(address, NULL, 16);

07.title: Address Search via kallsyms
07.content:
Address Search via kallsyms

An easier way to find sys_call_table is to use the kallsyms mechanism.

What is kallsyms?

It's a kernel mechanism that stores a symbol table (function and variable names) and their addresses.

Using kallsyms_lookup_name

#include <linux/kallsyms.h>

unsigned long *syscall_table;

static int init(void) {
  syscall_table = (unsigned long *)kallsyms_lookup_name("sys_call_table");
  if (syscall_table) {
    printk(KERN_INFO "sys_call_table found at %px\n", syscall_table);
  } else {
    printk(KERN_ERR "sys_call_table not found!\n");
    return -1;
  }
  return 0;
}

Advantages

  • Simpler than reading System.map
  • No file opening required
  • Works on most modern kernels

Requirements

  • Kernel must be built with CONFIG_KALLSYMS=y
  • Usually enabled by default

08.title: Interception with kprobes
08.content:
Interception with kprobes

Kprobes is a modern and safe way to intercept system calls.

How kprobe Works

  1. Register a kprobe on a function
  2. The kernel replaces the first instruction with int 3 (breakpoint)
  3. When the function is called, the processor hits the breakpoint
  4. Our handler is called
  5. Then the original instruction is executed

sys_openat Interception Code

#include <linux/kprobes.h>

static struct kprobe kp;

static int handler_pre(struct kprobe *p, struct pt_regs *regs) {
  const char __user *filename = (const char __user *)regs->si;
  char fname[256];
  
  if (strncpy_from_user(fname, filename, sizeof(fname) - 1) > 0) {
    printk(KERN_INFO "[kprobe] openat called for: %s\n", fname);
  }
  return 0;
}

static int __init kprobe_init(void) {
  kp.symbol_name = "sys_openat";
  kp.pre_handler = handler_pre;
  if (register_kprobe(&kp) < 0) {
    printk(KERN_ERR "Failed to register kprobe\n");
    return -1;
  }
  return 0;
}

Advantages over Direct Substitution

  • No memory protection bypass required (CR0)
  • Does not modify sys_call_table
  • Safer
  • Built-in kernel mechanism

09.title: Result Analysis with kretprobe
09.content:
Result Analysis with kretprobe

Kretprobe allows intercepting function exit and getting the return value.

How kretprobe Works

Intercepts the moment when the function completes and allows analyzing the result.

Code with kretprobe

#include <linux/kprobes.h>

static struct kretprobe rp;

static int ret_handler(struct kretprobe_instance *ri, struct pt_regs *regs) {
  long retval = regs_return_value(regs);
  
  if (retval < 0) {
    printk(KERN_INFO "[kretprobe] openat error: %ld\n", retval);
  } else {
    printk(KERN_INFO "[kretprobe] openat returned fd: %ld\n", retval);
  }
  return 0;
}

static int __init retprobe_init(void) {
  rp.kp.symbol_name = "sys_openat";
  rp.handler = ret_handler;
  rp.maxactive = 20;
  
  if (register_kretprobe(&rp) < 0) {
    printk(KERN_ERR "Failed to register kretprobe\n");
    return -1;
  }
  return 0;
}

When to Use

  • Tracking operation success
  • Monitoring return values
  • File open auditing

10.title: Approach Comparison and Conclusions
10.content:
Comparison of System Call Interception Approaches

1. Direct Substitution in sys_call_table

  • Pros: Simplicity, clarity
  • Cons: Memory protection bypass, dangerous, unsafe

2. Dynamic Address Resolution

  • Pros: Portability between kernel versions
  • Cons: More complex to implement

3. Using kallsyms

  • Pros: Simplicity, no file reading required
  • Cons: Requires CONFIG_KALLSYMS

4. Kprobes / Kretprobes

  • Pros: Safe, built-in mechanism, doesn't modify table
  • Cons: Not suitable for behavior modification

Recommendations

  • For learning: All three approaches
  • For production: Only kprobes
  • For experiments: Direct substitution
